title: Georgia School Shooter's Father Gets 15 Years in Landmark Sentencing
excerpt: Colin Gray, the first U.S. parent convicted of murder for a child's school shooting, was sentenced Thursday after a judge told him he 'failed as a parent' by ignoring escalating warning signs.
body:
• Colin Gray, 55, sentenced to 15 years in prison for providing his son the AR-15 used to kill four people at Apalachee High School in 2024
  • Judge told Gray "the warning lights were flashing brighter and brighter" before the Sept. 4, 2024 massacre that killed two students and two teachers
  • Gray is the first parent in U.S. history convicted of murder for a mass shooting committed by their child
  • The case follows the Crumbley convictions in Michigan and signals a growing legal strategy to hold parents accountable for school shootings

A Georgia judge sentenced Colin Gray to 15 years in prison on Thursday for providing his troubled teenage son the rifle used to kill four people at Apalachee High School in Winder, Georgia, in September 2024.

Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm handed down the sentence two days after Gray's son, Colt Gray, 16, received life in prison without parole for the shooting. Prosecutors had sought 80 years for the father; the defense asked for 20.

"It is clear you failed as a parent. The warning lights were flashing brighter and brighter, and you didn't get him help and you didn't remove his access to the guns."

— Judge Nicholas Primm, Barrow County Superior Court

First Parent Convicted of Murder for a School Shooting

Colin Gray, 55, was convicted in March on 27 counts — including second-degree murder, involuntary manslaughter, reckless conduct, and cruelty to children — after less than two hours of jury deliberation. Prosecutors argued he gave his 14-year-old son an AR-15-style rifle as a Christmas present despite mounting concerns about the teenager's mental health.

https://x.com/CBSNews/status/2082950284246937764

The case marked the first time in U.S. history that a parent was convicted of murder — rather than lesser charges — for a mass shooting carried out by their child. It follows the 2024 conviction of Jennifer and James Crumbley in Michigan, who received 10 to 15 years for involuntary manslaughter after their son killed four classmates at Oxford High School in 2021.

Judge Primm acknowledged the "divisive nature of the case" but noted the distinction between the father's negligence and his son's actions. "The loss here is profound," Primm said. "But I still have to distinguish your acts from the malignant heart and the acts that Colt Gray committed."

Warning Signs and a Chaotic Home Life

Evidence presented during the trial and sentencing painted a picture of a family in crisis. In May 2023, the local sheriff's office interviewed Colt Gray after anonymous tips about online threats of a school shooting. Colin Gray told authorities he had hunting guns at home but insisted his son did not have unsupervised access — a claim prosecutors later disputed.

District Attorney Brad Smith showed the judge a replica of Colt's bedroom wall, which featured a shrine to the gunman behind the 2018 Parkland, Florida, massacre. The risk was "staring him in the face every day," Smith told the court. Prosecutors also revealed that Colt had been active in an online group called the True Crime Community, where he became "obsessed" with school shooters.

Candice Broce, the head of the Georgia Division of Family and Children Services, testified that the family had an "extensive history" with the agency, including substantiated allegations of inadequate supervision, domestic violence, and failure to secure weapons.

Victims' Families Demand Maximum Punishment

Students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14, and teachers Richard Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53, were killed in the rampage. Nine others were wounded.

During emotional testimony, victims' family members urged the maximum sentence. Shayna Aspinwall, the widow of slain math teacher and football coach Richard Aspinwall, called Gray a "pathetic excuse for a father." Nautica Walton, who was shot in the leg during the attack, addressed the court directly.

"You took away the innocence of so many kids in that classroom that day, just because of what you were going through."

— Nautica Walton, shooting survivor

Colin Gray declined to speak at his sentencing and called no witnesses on his behalf.

A Legal Precedent Takes Shape

Defense attorney Brian Hobbs argued for a 20-year sentence — 10 years in prison and 10 on probation — comparable to the Crumbley case in Michigan. He urged the court "not to make Georgia the national outlier" in parent accountability cases.

But legal experts told USA Today that Gray's conviction on more severe charges, including second-degree murder under a relatively new Georgia law, may encourage prosecutors nationwide to pursue similar cases. Under Georgia law, second-degree murder carries up to 30 years — significantly more than involuntary manslaughter.

The 15-year sentence was imposed on the second-degree murder conviction, with all other sentences running concurrently. None of the charges carried mandatory prison time, giving Judge Primm wide discretion.

The twin sentencings — life for the shooter, 15 years for the parent who armed him — mark another chapter in an evolving legal strategy to address America's school shooting epidemic by holding adults accountable for children's access to firearms.
nri_angle: The case raises questions about gun safety and parental responsibility in the U.S., issues of particular concern for Indian-American families navigating school safety in their communities.
